scenes.visual: Title card 'Ten Years at Cedar Creek' over an aerial cartoon of a grid of square prairie plots. Same colour map as the first film. COLOUR MAP, same in both films: species A = GOLD; species B = TEAL; further species = CORAL, SLATE BLUE and SAND; complementarity = GREEN bar; selection = VIOLET bar; a plot's total biomass = a DARK OUTLINE drawn around the stacked species bars; the expected (monoculture-based) yield = a DASHED grey bar. Cream background, 16:9. Every number appears only as on-screen text. Plants are simple cartoons; bars computed from the stated numbers are labelled 'computed'; anything else is labelled 'schematic'.

scenes.tts: The first film showed a field as a sum of its species. Now follow one real field for a decade. How much of its extra yield is complementarity, and how much is selection? Does the answer change as the plots age?
scenes.visual: Brief recap: the first film's stacked bar (GOLD under TEAL, DARK OUTLINE) above the DASHED expected bar, the gap bracketed 'extra yield'. The bracket splits into a GREEN half and a VIOLET half with a question mark between them, then the scene pulls back to the aerial plot grid.
scenes.narration: The first film showed a field as a sum of its species. Now follow one real field for a decade. How much of its extra yield is complementarity, and how much is selection? Does the answer change as the plots age?

scenes.tts: The field is Cedar Creek, in Minnesota. In spring nineteen ninety-four, David Tilman and colleagues sowed a hundred and sixty-eight plots there. Each plot was nine metres on a side.
scenes.visual: A map pin on Minnesota labelled 'Cedar Creek'. The plot grid fills in square by square; counter '168 plots'; one square outlined 'each 9 m by 9 m'; date tag 'sown spring 1994'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: The field is Cedar Creek, in Minnesota. In spring nineteen ninety-four, David Tilman and colleagues sowed a hundred and sixty-eight plots there. Each plot was nine metres on a side.

scenes.tts: Each plot got one, two, four, eight or sixteen species. They were drawn at random from a pool of eighteen grassland and savanna species. Every plot got the same seed mass.
scenes.visual: A tray of 18 plant icons. For each plot, a die rolls and icons hop from the tray into it; columns labelled 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 species. A small seed bag of identical size drops onto every plot: 'same seed mass in every plot'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Each plot got one, two, four, eight or sixteen species. They were drawn at random from a pool of eighteen grassland and savanna species. Every plot got the same seed mass.

scenes.tts: Because the draw was random, nobody chose strong species for the rich plots. Better soil could line up with richness only by chance.
scenes.visual: A hand reaching to pick a large tuft for a 16-species plot is crossed out. Faint soil-colour patches under the grid are scattered at random, unevenly, across the richness columns; label 'soil not systematically aligned with richness'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Because the draw was random, nobody chose strong species for the rich plots. Better soil could line up with richness only by chance.

scenes.tts: Every year the plants were clipped, dried and weighed. Year after year, plots with more species generally grew more aboveground biomass.
scenes.visual: Year counter runs through the decade. Five bars, one per richness level (1, 2, 4, 8, 16 species), each a DARK OUTLINE filled with stacked species colours, stay ordered short to tall as the years tick. Axis 'aboveground biomass'. Labelled 'schematic, not data'.
scenes.narration: Every year the plants were clipped, dried and weighed. Year after year, plots with more species generally grew more aboveground biomass.

scenes.tts: Joseph Fargione and colleagues then split the extra yield in each year, using every species' yield in mixture and alone. The green bar is complementarity. The violet bar is selection.
scenes.visual: Beside the year counter a pair of bars appears for each year from 1996: GREEN 'complementarity', VIOLET 'selection', on an axis with a zero line. Name tag 'Fargione and colleagues, 2007'. Labelled 'schematic: direction of change only'.
scenes.narration: Joseph Fargione and colleagues then split the extra yield in each year, using every species' yield in mixture and alone. The green bar is complementarity. The violet bar is selection.

scenes.tts: In the early years, selection was positive. Rich plots outyielded poor ones partly because they more often held a productive species.
scenes.visual: Early years: the VIOLET bars stand clearly above zero. In the 16-species plot icon, one oversized tuft glows. Label 'early: selection positive'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: In the early years, selection was positive. Rich plots outyielded poor ones partly because they more often held a productive species.

scenes.tts: Then the balance shifted toward complementarity. Selection shrank, crossed zero and ended strongly negative. Now the biggest gains went to species that yield little alone. The extra biomass came to be associated with more nitrogen held in the plants.
scenes.visual: Years tick to 2005: VIOLET bars shrink, cross the zero line and grow downward to a large negative bar; GREEN bars take up the positive side. On-screen 'by 2005: selection strongly negative' and 'biggest relative-yield gains: species small in monoculture'. A small plant icon with an 'N' label: 'associated with larger plant nitrogen pools'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Then the balance shifted toward complementarity. Selection shrank, crossed zero and ended strongly negative. Now the biggest gains went to species that yield little alone. The extra biomass came to be associated with more nitrogen held in the plants.

scenes.tts: So the same plots gave a different answer depending on which years you looked at. Each year's split is a snapshot, and the snapshots changed.
scenes.visual: Two snapshots of the GREEN and VIOLET bars, 'early years' and 'late years', slide side by side; the VIOLET bar points up in one and down in the other. Schematic.
scenes.narration: So the same plots gave a different answer depending on which years you looked at. Each year's split is a snapshot, and the snapshots changed.

scenes.tts: Now zoom into the sixteen-species plots and follow their species. On average, each species swings proportionally more from year to year than species in poorer plots.
scenes.visual: Zoom into one plot. Its species bars (GOLD, TEAL, CORAL, SLATE BLUE, SAND and more) bounce through the years; beside them, a species from a one-species plot bounces less, relative to its size. Label 'species, on average: less steady in rich plots'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: Now zoom into the sixteen-species plots and follow their species. On average, each species swings proportionally more from year to year than species in poorer plots.

scenes.tts: So the parts became less steady, on average. Will the plot's total be more steady, or less steady, than a monoculture's?
scenes.visual: The bouncing freezes. The DARK OUTLINE around the stacked species glows; option tags 'more steady' and 'less steady' float beside it.
scenes.narration: So the parts became less steady, on average. Will the plot's total be more steady, or less steady, than a monoculture's?

scenes.visual: Hold the frame; a 5-second countdown; caption 'Predict: is the total steadier?'

scenes.tts: More steady. Tilman, Peter Reich and Johannes Knops reported this in two thousand six. The total varied proportionally less, even though its species, on average, varied more.
scenes.visual: Animation resumes: the species bars keep jittering while the DARK OUTLINE moves only gently, beside a monoculture bar that swings hard. Name tag 'Tilman, Reich and Knops, Nature, 2006'. Label 'total: steadier; species: less steady'. Schematic.
scenes.narration: More steady. Tilman, Peter Reich and Johannes Knops reported this in two thousand six. The total varied proportionally less, even though its species, on average, varied more.

scenes.tts: Did opposite swings grow stronger in richer plots? Their analysis found no evidence of that. Averaging, together with a higher mean, explained the steadier total. A higher mean helps only if the swings grow less than in proportion.
scenes.visual: Two tags light up next to the calm outline: 'swings partly cancel (averaging)' and 'higher mean biomass'. A third tag, 'covariance effect: opposite swings growing with richness', appears greyed with 'no evidence found'.
scenes.narration: Did opposite swings grow stronger in richer plots? Their analysis found no evidence of that. Averaging, together with a higher mean, explained the steadier total. A higher mean helps only if the swings grow less than in proportion.

scenes.tts: Assigned at random and watched for a decade, richer plots grew more and grew steadier. Their species, on average, grew less steady.
scenes.visual: Recap: the five richness bars ordered short to tall; the calm outline of the 16-species total beside its jittering species bars.
scenes.narration: Assigned at random and watched for a decade, richer plots grew more and grew steadier. Their species, on average, grew less steady.

scenes.visual: End card, one line only: 'Richer plots: more, steadier biomass, though species were less steady on average.'
